title: Two News Stories From Abroad Suggest American Education Is on the Wrong Track
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler uses two recent foreign news stories to question the progressive, constructivist orthodoxy of American teacher training. She first sets out the cognitive-science case that explicit instruction works best, especially for novices, and that most schools sit on a spectrum rather than at either pole. The first story is the first GCSE results of England's Michaela Community School, a strict, explicit-instruction school that far exceeded national averages with low-income students. The second is Finland, whose 2016 move to student-centred curriculum has coincided with declining PISA scores and complaints about pupils left to manage themselves. She concedes two stories prove nothing, but argues progressive methods mainly suit already-knowledgeable self-starters while most children thrive with explicit instruction.
points: The effective default for novices is explicit instruction, yet teacher training in English-speaking countries teaches the opposite.
Michaela's first GCSE results, from low-income students in a knowledge-heavy, explicit-instruction school, far exceeded national averages.
Finland's admired decentralised system was actually built on earlier centralised control, and its slide followed adoption of progressive principles.
A Finnish pupil's account shows how self-directed planning can leave struggling children feeling they learned nothing.
Progressive methods tend to widen gaps because they work best for students who already have knowledge and support.
quotes: Few if any schools embrace one of these approaches to the exclusion of the other. Virtually any teacher, no matter how “progressive,” provides some information directly. Similarly, even the most “traditional” teachers undoubtedly allow for some inquiry and knowledge-construction on the part of their students. It’s more a question of where the balance lies and what teachers feel they should be doing.

Five years ago Birbalsingh founded a new school, the Michaela Community School, that embraces the idea that the teacher should stand in front of a class and explicitly impart information. The school also enthusiastically flouts other progressive education tenets: students are required to memorize historical dates and poetry, for example, and homework consists largely of self-quizzing.

The news this week was that Michaela had gotten its first round of results on national exams known as the GCSEs, taken by students when they’re 15 or 16. Michaela’s students, all of them low-income and many of color, did far better than the national average: 18% of the exams received the top grade, a 9, as compared to 4.5% of exams nationwide; 54% received a 7, 8 or 9—equivalent to an A or A+—as opposed to the national average of 22%.
But that’s just what the system looked like in the early 2000s. Reformers overlooked the fact that in earlier years, there had been quite a bit of centralized control

Last week’s news story focused on complaints about one Finnish elementary school, an early adopter of the new approach, where students are expected to take responsibility for creating and adhering to their own personal weekly plans and remembering the dates of exams and deadlines.

They can work well for conscientious self-starters who have already managed to acquire a fair amount of academic knowledge—perhaps from their well-educated parents. But arguably, those students will learn no matter what methods are used. Schools need to take into account the far greater number of children who will only thrive with explicit instruction.
